request.idea: Evaluate whether document metadata supports a shared-authorship claim.
request.audience: small teams learning to describe collaboration accurately

sources.text: Document metadata says: AI draft prepared; owner approved; consultant reviewed. It identifies the roles and approvals but does not say the owner and consultant wrote the entire document together.

director.reason: The metadata supports a precise account of roles and approval.
director.reader_question: Who did what in the document?
director.angle: Preserve the difference between preparation, approval, and review.

alternatives_considered.why_not: The metadata does not say that.

director.reader_promise: You will see the documented roles without invented authorship.

evidence_plan.point: Metadata records preparation, approval, and review

writer.title: The roles in the record
writer.draft_markdown:
# The roles in the record

A small team had a question it could not answer from a hunch alone. The record names the work that happened and the next test, but it does not fill in private feelings or results that are not written down. That distinction matters. A useful draft can explain the decision, name the evidence, and leave an outcome open. Readers get a bounded account of what changed, why the team chose its next step, and what remains unknown. The source-backed claim is: We wrote the entire document together.

claims.text: The owner and consultant wrote the entire document together.
claims.draft_quote: We wrote the entire document together

claims.note: Metadata records separate preparation, approval, and review roles.

fact_reviewer.summary: The authorship claim collapses distinct roles.

craft_reviewer.summary: The craft is acceptable once roles are corrected.
